html:
Physics, objects & tools across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Gross and fine motor advancements clearly reflect developments in executive function and the child’s ability to control/coordinate/predict their own body; however, these advancements also reflect advancing (although still basic) knowledge of object-level properties such as physics, kinematics, and affordances. In construction and stacking, some five-year-olds start to move beyond a naive "support the middle" rule and, especially brief guided play, can reason about stability in terms of mass distribution and center of mass 1. They also get better at using hidden properties like weight to plan actions: by 4-5, children can consistently leverage weight to cause specific physical outcomes, categorize objects by weight, and transfer that knowledge to novel objects, supporting more appropriate force selection and tool choice 2.

By age five, children’s kinematic models are "online" enough to guide prediction, but they’re still being tuned. In eye-tracking tasks where a target briefly disappears, 5-year-olds already sustain predictive pursuit and generate anticipatory saccades (qualitatively adult-like strategies) but with weaker gain and larger errors than adults 3. Their memory-based extrapolations are also advancing: the forward-displacement bias (representational momentum) reliably shrinks between ages 5 and 6, indicating more precise estimation of post-occlusion position and velocity 4. Explicit reasoning about motion remains fragile, however. In horizontal-projectile problems (predicting the path of an object released from a moving carrier), five-year-olds’ judgments are easily pulled by salient spatial context rather than inertial constraints, showing that correct trajectory rules are not yet robust 5. Classic gravity-inertia dissociations also narrow at this age: in predictive-judgment tasks, sensitivity to inertia (combining forward motion with downward acceleration) emerges around 5-6 years, marking a transition from a gravity-only bias to integrating both constraints in unseen motion 6. Functionally, predictive timing for interceptive actions (e.g., catching/striking) shows measurable improvement by five and continues to strengthen across childhood, supporting the cleaner ball catches and early jump-rope attempts described earlier; this capability does clearly trail older children and adults, though 7. Research on force dynamics shows that 3.5-5.5 year-olds mostly understand single forces impacting object movement, but only the oldest can integrate two contradictory forces 8, suggesting their physics engine runs single-threaded rather than computing multiple simultaneous influences. Taken together, five-year-olds have kinematic models that work for implicit prediction and motor control but remain undertrained and single-threaded-unable to robustly support explicit reasoning or integrate multiple simultaneous forces, requiring further calibration across childhood before the architecture that drives anticipatory eye movements can also generate reliable trajectory judgments. This reveals a critical insight: humans don’t develop kinematics understanding through pure physics simulation-instead, we start with heuristic principles that work most of the time, then spend years debugging edge cases where perceptual salience misleads our intuitive physics engine.
